Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 27, verses 1–3:

The interpretation of the words of God Most High: ﴿Ta, Sin. These are the verses of the Qur'an and a Book that makes things clear. (1) A guidance and good tidings for the believers, (2) who establish the prayer and give the zakah, and who are certain of the Hereafter. (3)﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: We have already explained the matter in what has passed of this book, concerning the letters of the alphabet that open the surahs, and ﴿Ta, Sin﴾ is among them. It has been transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that his words ﴿Ta, Sin﴾ are an oath that God swore, and that it is one of the names of God.

Narrated to me by 'Ali ibn Dawud, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih told us, who said: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas: concerning His words ﴿Ta, Sin﴾, it is an oath that God swore, and it is one of the names of God.

According to this view, its meaning is: "By the All-Hearing, the Subtle, these are the verses that We have sent down to you, O Muhammad, verses of the Qur'an and of a Book that makes things clear." That is, it makes clear to whoever reflects upon it and considers it with understanding that it is from God, sent down to you. You did not invent it, nor did you fabricate it, nor did anyone else among God's creation, because no one among the creatures is able to produce its like, even if the jinn and mankind were to band together to do so. The words ﴿and a Book that makes things clear﴾ are in the genitive (khafd) by way of coordination with "the Qur'an."

* *

As for His words ﴿guidance﴾:

It is a description of the Qur'an.

It means: these are the verses of the Qur'an, a clarification from God by which He makes clear the path of truth and the way of peace. ﴿And good tidings for the believers﴾ means: and a glad tiding for those who believe in it and affirm what was sent down in it, of the great success in the Hereafter.

Regarding His words ﴿guidance and good tidings﴾ there are two readings in Arabic grammar: the nominative (raf'), as a predicate beginning a sentence, meaning "it is guidance and good tidings"; and the accusative (nasb), as a circumstantial state (qat') of "the verses of the Qur'an," so that the meaning is: "These are the verses of the Qur'an, guidance and good tidings for the believers." Then the alif and lam were dropped from "guidance" (al-huda) and "good tidings" (al-bushra), so they became indefinite, and since they are descriptions of a definite noun, they were put in the accusative.

* *

As for His words ﴿who establish the prayer﴾ (alladhina yuqimuna al-salah):

It means: it is guidance and good tidings for whoever believes in it and establishes the obligatory prayer with its prescribed limits.

* *

As for His words ﴿and give the zakah﴾ (wa yu'tuna al-zakah):

It means: and they pay the obligatory zakah. It has also been said that it means: they purify their bodies from the filth of sins.

We have already explained this earlier in a way that suffices without repeating it in this place. ﴿And they are certain of the Hereafter﴾ means: and they, along with their establishing of the prayer and giving of the obligatory zakah, are certain of the return to God after death. Therefore they humble themselves in obedience to God, hoping for His abundant reward and fearing His severe punishment. They are not like those who deny the resurrection and are indifferent whether they do good or evil, whether they obey or disobey, for if they do good they hope for no reward, and if they do evil they fear no punishment.

* *

The Exalted says: These who do not believe in the Hereafter, for them is the worst torment in this world, and they are those who were killed at Badr from among the polytheists of Quraysh.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, you [O Muhammad] are receiving the Qur'an from the Presence of One who is Wise and Knowing.(6) [Mention] when Moses said to his family, "Indeed, I have perceived a fire. I will bring you from it information or bring you a burning brand that you may warm yourselves."(7) But when he reached it, he was called, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it. And exalted is Allah, Lord of the worlds.(8)﴾

The Exalted says: And indeed you, O Muhammad, are memorizing the Qur'an and learning it ﴿from the Presence of One who is Wise and Knowing﴾. That is: from the presence of One who is Wise in managing His creation, Knowing of the news of His creation and their welfare, and of what will occur of their affairs, and what has passed of their reports, and what is newly arising among them. ﴿When Moses said﴾ "When" is connected to "Knowing." The meaning of the sentence is: He is Knowing when Moses said ﴿to his family﴾, while he was journeying from Madyan to Egypt, and the cold of their night had troubled them when his firestone failed to kindle. ﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾, that is, I have seen a fire or sensed it, so remain where you are. ﴿I will bring you from it information﴾, meaning from the fire, the pronoun and the feminine reference refer to the fire. ﴿Or I will bring you a burning brand﴾

The readers differed concerning the recitation of this. The majority of the readers of Medina and Basra recited "bi-shihābi qabasin" with the word shihāb construed as annexed to qabas, without tanwīn, meaning: or I will bring you a flame of fire that I take a brand from. The majority of the readers of Kufa recited ﴿bi-shihābin qabasin﴾ with tanwīn on shihāb and without annexing it to qabas, meaning: or I will bring you a kindled brand.

The correct view on this is that both are well-known recitations among the reciters of the regions, close in meaning, so whichever one the reciter reads is correct. Some grammarians of Basra said: if qabas is made a substitute for shihāb, then shihāb takes tanwīn, and if shihāb is annexed to qabas, shihāb does not take tanwīn. Some grammarians of Kufa said: if shihāb is annexed to qabas, it is like His saying ﴿and the Abode of the Hereafter﴾, which is annexed to itself when its two names and wordings differ, and the second is thought to be other than the first. He said: similar to it are "ḥabbat al-khaḍrā'" (the green grain), "laylat al-qamrā'" (the moonlit night), "yawm al-Khamīs" (Thursday), and what resembles them. Another of them said: if shihāb is qabas itself, annexation is not permissible, because qabas is a qualifier, and a noun is not annexed to its qualifier except in rare speech; yet it has come: ﴿and the Abode of the Hereafter﴾ and ﴿and indeed the Abode of the Hereafter﴾.

The correct view on this: if shihāb is intended to be other than qabas, then the recitation with annexation is correct, because the meaning of the sentence then is what we have explained, that it is a flame of a brand, as the poet said:

In his hand is a straight, well-trimmed spear, in which is a point like the flame of a brand.

[The line is among the witnesses of Abu 'Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an, folio 175, where he said: "bi-shihāb qabas" means a flame of fire. The majāz of qabas is what is taken from it and from the embers.]

And if shihāb is intended to be qabas itself, or a qualifier of it, then the correct reading for shihāb is with tanwīn, because the sound usage of the Arabs is to avoid annexing a noun to its qualifier or to itself; rather, the known annexations in their speech are of a thing to something other than itself and other than its qualifier.

* *

His saying: ﴿So that you may warm yourselves﴾

That is: so that you may warm yourselves by it from the cold.

* *

His saying: ﴿But when he came to it﴾

That is: when Moses came to the fire that he had perceived, ﴿he was called, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it"﴾.

As reported:

⁕ Ali narrated to us, saying: Abdullah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿he was called, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire"﴾: he says: sanctified.

The people of interpretation differed concerning who is meant by His saying ﴿whoever is in the fire﴾. Some said: the Exalted meant by it Himself, who was in the fire, and the fire was His light, the Exalted, according to a group of the people of interpretation.

Those who said that:

⁕ Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿but when he came to it, he was called, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire"﴾, meaning Himself; he said: the light of the Lord of the worlds was in the tree.

⁕ Isma'il ibn al-Haytham Abu al-'Aliya al-'Abdi narrated to me, saying: Abu Qutayba narrated to us, from Warqa', from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding God's saying ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾: he said: He called him while he was in the fire.

⁕ al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Sufyan narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying ﴿he was called, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it"﴾: he said: it is the light.

Ma'mar said: Qatada said: ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾: he said: the light of God, blessed.

⁕ He said: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: al-Hasan al-Basri said: ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾ [The author perhaps did not state the content of the saying, relying on the preceding text since it agrees with it in wording and meaning. He did this in several places.]

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: the fire was blessed.

Those who said that:

⁕ al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Ashyab narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿he was called, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire"﴾: the fire was blessed. Thus said Ibn Abbas.

⁕ Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿that blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾: he said: the fire was blessed.

⁕ al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Mujahid said: ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾: he said: the fire was blessed.

⁕ Muhammad ibn Sinan al-Qazzaz narrated to us, saying: Makki ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: Musa narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, regarding His saying ﴿that blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾: the light of the Most Merciful, and the Light is God. ﴿And exalted is God, Lord of the worlds﴾.

The people of interpretation differed about the meaning of "fire" in this place. Some said: its meaning is light, as I have mentioned from those I cited for that.

Others said: its meaning is fire, not light.

Those who said that:

⁕ al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: the veil of might, the veil of the King, the veil of the sultan, and the veil of the fire, which is that fire from which he was called. He said: and the veil of light, the veil of the cloud, and the veil of water. It was only said "Blessed is whoever is in the fire" and not "Blessed be in whoever is in the fire," according to the dialect of those who say "bārakaka Allāh" (God blesses you). The Arabs say "bārakaka Allāh" and "bāraka fīka" (God blesses in you).

* *

His saying: ﴿And whoever is around it﴾

That is: and whoever is around the fire. It was said: by "whoever is around it" is meant the angels.

Those who said that:

⁕ Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿and whoever is around it﴾: he said: meaning the angels.

⁕ al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from al-Hasan, the like of it.

Others said: it is Moses and the angels.

⁕ Muhammad ibn Sinan al-Qazzaz narrated to us, saying: Makki ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: Musa narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b: ﴿and whoever is around it﴾: he said: Moses the Prophet and the angels; then He said: "O Moses, indeed I am God, the Mighty, the Wise" (Qur'an 27:9).

He said: similar to it are "ḥabbat al-khaḍrā'" (the green grain), "laylat al-qamrā'" (the moonlit night), "yawm al-Khamīs" (Thursday), and what resembles them. Another of them said: if shihāb is qabas itself, annexation is not permissible, because qabas is a qualifier, and a noun is not annexed to its qualifier except in rare speech; yet it has come: ﴿and the Abode of the Hereafter﴾ and ﴿and indeed the Abode of the Hereafter﴾.

The correct view on this: if shihāb is intended to be other than qabas, then the recitation with annexation is correct, because the meaning of the sentence then is what we have explained, that it is a flame of a brand, as the poet said:

In his hand is a straight, well-trimmed spear, in which is a point like the flame of a brand.

[The line is among the witnesses of Abu 'Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an, folio 175, where he said: "bi-shihāb qabas" means a flame of fire. The majāz of qabas is what is taken from it and from the embers.]

And if shihāb is intended to be qabas itself, or a qualifier of it, then the correct reading for shihāb is with tanwīn, because the sound usage of the Arabs is to avoid annexing a noun to its qualifier or to itself; rather, the known annexations in their speech are of a thing to something other than itself and other than its qualifier.

* *

His saying: ﴿So that you may warm yourselves﴾

That is: so that you may warm yourselves by it from the cold.

* *

His saying: ﴿But when he came to it﴾

That is: when Moses came to the fire that he had perceived, ﴿he was called, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it"﴾.

As reported:

⁕ Ali narrated to us, saying: Abdullah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿he was called, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire"﴾: he says: sanctified.

The people of interpretation differed concerning who is meant by His saying ﴿whoever is in the fire﴾. Some said: the Exalted meant by it Himself, who was in the fire, and the fire was His light, the Exalted, according to a group of the people of interpretation.

Those who said that:

⁕ Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿but when he came to it, he was called, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire"﴾, meaning Himself; he said: the light of the Lord of the worlds was in the tree.

⁕ Isma'il ibn al-Haytham Abu al-'Aliya al-'Abdi narrated to me, saying: Abu Qutayba narrated to us, from Warqa', from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding God's saying ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾: he said: He called him while he was in the fire.

⁕ al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Sufyan narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying ﴿he was called, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it"﴾: he said: it is the light.

Ma'mar said: Qatada said: ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾: he said: the light of God, blessed.

⁕ He said: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: al-Hasan al-Basri said: ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾ [The author perhaps did not state the content of the saying, relying on the preceding text since it agrees with it in wording and meaning. He did this in several places.]

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: the fire was blessed.

Those who said that:

⁕ al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Ashyab narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿he was called, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire"﴾: the fire was blessed. Thus said Ibn Abbas.

⁕ Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿that blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾: he said: the fire was blessed.

⁕ al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Mujahid said: ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾: he said: the fire was blessed.

⁕ Muhammad ibn Sinan al-Qazzaz narrated to us, saying: Makki ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: Musa narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, regarding His saying ﴿that blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾: the light of the Most Merciful, and the Light is God. ﴿And exalted is God, Lord of the worlds﴾.

The people of interpretation differed about the meaning of "fire" in this place. Some said: its meaning is light, as I have mentioned from those I cited for that.

Others said: its meaning is fire, not light.

Those who said that:

⁕ al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: the veil of might, the veil of the King, the veil of the sultan, and the veil of the fire, which is that fire from which he was called. He said: and the veil of light, the veil of the cloud, and the veil of water. It was only said "Blessed is whoever is in the fire" and not "Blessed be in whoever is in the fire," according to the dialect of those who say "bārakaka Allāh" (God blesses you). The Arabs say "bārakaka Allāh" and "bāraka fīka" (God blesses in you).

* *

His saying: ﴿And whoever is around it﴾

That is: and whoever is around the fire. It was said: by "whoever is around it" is meant the angels.

Those who said that:

⁕ Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿and whoever is around it﴾: he said: meaning the angels.

⁕ al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from al-Hasan, the like of it.

Others said: it is Moses and the angels.

⁕ Muhammad ibn Sinan al-Qazzaz narrated to us, saying: Makki ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: Musa narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b: ﴿and whoever is around it﴾: he said: Moses the Prophet and the angels; then He said: "O Moses, indeed I am God, the Mighty, the Wise" (Qur'an 27:9).

* *

His saying: ﴿And exalted is God, Lord of the worlds﴾

That is: and glorification of God, Lord of the worlds, from what the wrongdoers attribute to Him.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 9–11:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Moses, indeed it is I, Allah, the Almighty, the Wise﴾ (9) ﴿And throw down your staff.﴾ So when he saw it moving as if it were a snake (jann), he turned back in retreat and did not return. ﴿O Moses, do not fear. Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾ (10) ﴿except one who has wronged; then substitutes good after evil — indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (11)

He, exalted is His remembrance, says, reporting His speech to Moses: ﴿Indeed, it is I, Allah, the Almighty﴾ in His vengeance against His enemies, ﴿the Wise﴾ in His management of His creation. The particle ha' in His saying ﴿innahu﴾ is the hā' of ʿimād (the pronoun of support, dummy pronoun), and it is a word that does not appear in the view of some of the people of Arabic grammar. And one of the grammarians of Kufa said: it is the unknown hā' (hā' al-majhūla), and its meaning is: the matter and the affair is: I am Allah.

* *

And His saying: ﴿And throw down your staff. So when he saw it moving﴾

In the speech there is an omitted element whose mention has been left out, being sufficed by what is mentioned over what has been omitted, and it is: so he threw it down, and it became a snake moving. ﴿So when he saw it moving as if it were a jann﴾ means: as if it were a great snake. And the jann is a species of snakes known.

Ibn Juraij said concerning this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, he said: Ibn Juraij said regarding ﴿And throw down your staff. So when he saw it moving as if it were a jann﴾: when it turned into a snake running. And this species of snakes is what the rajiz (poet) meant by his saying:

They raise, at night when it darkens, necks of jinn-snakes and trembling heads,
And a necks after the ar-rasim, swift (khaṭafā)

[These are three verses of mashtūr rajaz by al-Khaṭafī, who is Ḥudhayfa ibn Badr, grandfather of Jarir ibn ʿAṭiyya, the poet of Tamim, describing his camels and their march at night. Asdafa: grew dark. The jannān is a species of snakes which, when they move, raise their heads; and the hāmm is the plural of hāmma. The rujaf is the plural of rājifa, i.e. agitated, because of their trembling in motion and speed. The ʿanaq is a kind of fast pace. The rasīm is a light pace. The khayṭaf is quick; it is also narrated as khaṭafā, and with this Ḥudhayfa, grandfather of Jarir, was given the epithet al-Khaṭafī, because the word came in his poetry and in (Lisān, kh-ṭ-f). The khayṭafī means the quickness of the pace being pulled, as if it snatches its neck in its walk, i.e. drags it; and a camel khayṭaf means swift in passing, and it is said ʿanaq khayṭaf and khaṭafī; the grandfather of Jarir said: "and a neck after the rasīm, khayṭafā". It was also said that it derives from al-khaṭf, which is snatching, and a camel khayṭaf is one whose pace is like that, i.e. swift in passing.]]

And His saying: ﴿He turned back in retreat﴾ means, He, exalted is His remembrance: Moses turned away fleeeing in fear of it. ﴿And did not return﴾ means: he did not come back. From the saying of the people: ʿaqaba fulān, when he returned upon his heels to where he started.

And in accordance with what we have said regarding the interpretation of this, the people of interpretation said.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, he said: Abu ʿĀṣim narrated to us, he said: ʿĪsā narrated to us; and al-Ḥārith narrated to me, he said: al-Ḥasan narrated to us, he said: Warqāʾ narrated to us, all of them, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of God: ﴿And did not return﴾, he said: he did not return.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, similarly.

He said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Abu Sufyan narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatada, he said: he did not look back.

Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿And did not return﴾, he said: he did not return. ﴿O Moses﴾, he said: when he threw down the staff it became a snake, so he was frightened by it and became distressed, so God said: ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾. He said: so he did not heed that. He said: So God said to him: ﴿Come forward and do not fear; indeed, you are among the secure﴾. He said: so he did not stop at any of this until He said: ﴿We will return it to its original form﴾. He said: so he looked, and behold, it was a staff as it had been, so he returned and took it, and then he became strong after that until he was sending it against Pharaoh and taking it.

* *

And His saying: ﴿O Moses, do not fear. Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence, except one who has wronged﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: So his Lord called to him: O Moses, do not fear this snake; indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence. He means: indeed, My messengers and prophets whom I have singled out with prophethood do not fear in My presence, except whoever among them has wronged, acting otherwise than what He permitted him to act upon.

And in accordance with what we have said regarding this, the people of interpretation said.

Mention of those who said that:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, he said: regarding His saying: ﴿O Moses, do not fear; indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾, he said: God does not frighten the prophets except for a sin that one of them commits; if he commits it, He frightens him until He takes it from him.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: ʿAbd Allah al-Fazari narrated to us, from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubarak, from Abu Bakr, from al-Hasan, he said: regarding His saying: ﴿O Moses, do not fear; indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence, except one who has wronged﴾, he said: indeed I only frightened you because of your killing of a soul. He said: al-Hasan said: the prophets used to sin and then be punished.

The people of Arabic grammar differed over the reason for the use of "illā" (except) in this place, which is an exception with God's promise of forgiveness, excepted from His saying "indeed the messengers do not fear in My presence" with His saying "indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful". The rule of the exception is that what follows it be contrary to the meaning of what precedes it; that is, if what precedes it is negated affirmed, as in the saying: "no one stood except Zayd", Zayd is affirmed as standing, because he is excepted from what is before "illā", and what is before "illā" is negated of standing; and if what precedes it is affirmed, negated, as in the saying of people: "the people stood except Zayd"; Zayd is negated of standing, and its meaning: indeed Zayd did not stand, the people are affirmed as standing. ﴿Except one who has wronged, then substitutes good after evil﴾, so God has granted him security by His promise of forgiveness and mercy, and has placed him among the count of the messengers in whose presence no one fears. Some of the grammarians of Basra said: "illā" was used in this place because "illā" enters into such speech, like the saying of the Arabs: "I do not complain except of good", so he did not make His saying "except good" about complaint, but he knew that when he says "I do not complain of anything" he mentions good about himself; as if he said: "I do not mention except good".

And some of the grammarians of Kufa said: someone says: how is one who fears because of wrongdoing made, then substitutes good after evil, and he is forgiven? I say to you: in this verse there are two aspects. One is that the messengers are protected, forgiven, secure on the Day of Resurrection; and whoever mixed a righteous deed with another evil one, he fears and hopes; this is one aspect. The other: that the exception is made from those left out in the word, because the meaning is: the messengers do not fear in My presence; fear is only for those other than them; then He excepted, saying: ﴿except one who has wronged, then substitutes good﴾, meaning: he was a polytheist, then repented from polytheism and did good, so that one is forgiven and does not fear. He said: some grammarians have said: "illā" in the language is in the position of "wa" (and), and the meaning of this verse is: the messengers do not fear in My presence, nor one who has wronged then substituted good. He said: they made its like His saying: ﴿So that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who have wronged﴾. He said: and I did not find that Arabic admits what they said, because I do not permit: "the people stood except ʿAbd Allah", while ʿAbd Allah is standing; the meaning of the exception is that the noun after "illā" exits from the sense of the nouns before "illā". And I see it permissible for someone to say: "I owe you a thousand besides another thousand"; if "illā" is placed in this position it is correct, and "illā" is in the sense of what they said. As for it bare, having excepted a little of the much, then no; but like it is what the meaning of "illā" is like the meaning of "wa", and it is not it: His saying ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾ is in meaning: what your Lord wills of addition. So do not make "illā" in the position of "wa", but in the position of "siwā" (besides); for when "siwā" is in the place of "illā", it is correct in the sense of "wa", because you say: "I have much wealth besides this", i.e. and this is with me, as if you said: "I have much wealth and this also is with me"; and it is further in "siwā" than in "illā", because you say: "with me is besides this", and you do not say: "with me is except this".

Abu Jaʿfar said: The correct statement regarding His saying ﴿except one who has wronged, then substitutes﴾ in my view is other than what these people of Arabic whose sayings we have related said; rather it is the statement said by al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Juraij, and whoever said their statement, which is that His saying: ﴿except one who has been wronged﴾ is a correct exception from His saying ﴿the messengers do not fear in My presence, except one who has wronged﴾ among them, who committed a sin; for he is fearful in His presence of His punishment. And al-Hasan, may God have mercy on him, clarified the meaning of God's saying that to Moses, which is his saying: indeed I only frightened you because of your killing of a soul.

If someone says: what is the reasoning of His saying, if His saying ﴿except one who has been wronged﴾ is a correct exception and outside the count of those messengers who do not fear in His presence, and how can one who has been promised forgiveness and mercy be fearful? It is said: His saying ﴿then substitutes good after evil﴾ is another statement after the first, and the report about the messengers who wronged among them has ended, and about those among them who did not wrong at His saying ﴿except one who has been wronged﴾; then He began the report about those among the messengers who wronged, and the rest of people other than them; and it is said: so whoever wronged, then substituted good after evil, indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful to him.

If someone says: then why is "thumma" (then) attached if it is not a conjunction to His saying ﴿wronged﴾? It is said: it is upon something left out, sufficed by the indication of His saying ﴿then substitutes good after evil﴾ from mentioning it, since a similar thing has already occurred before in the speech, namely: "so whoever of creation wronged". As for those whose statements from the people of Arabic we have mentioned, they spoke according to the way of Arabic, except that they overlooked the meaning of the word and carried it upon other than its interpretive direction. Rather, speech should be carried upon its correct interpretive direction, and for its grammatical construction a sound outlet should be sought in that direction, not by diverting the word from its meaning and its correct interpretive direction.

And His saying: ﴿then substitutes good after evil﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: so whoever among God's creation commits wrongdoing and incurs sin, then substitutes good, i.e. then repents from that wrongdoing and incurring of sin, ﴿indeed I am Forgiving﴾, meaning: indeed I cover over his sin and that wrongdoing by My pardon, and by leaving off punishing him for it, ﴿Merciful﴾ to him, that I would punish him after his substituting good for its opposite.

And in accordance with what we have said regarding this, the people of interpretation said.

The rule of the exception is that what follows it be contrary to the meaning of what precedes it; that is, if what precedes it is negated affirmed, as in the saying: "no one stood except Zayd", Zayd is affirmed as standing, because he is excepted from what is before "illā", and what is before "illā" is negated of standing; and if what precedes it is affirmed, negated, as in the saying of people: "the people stood except Zayd"; Zayd is negated of standing, and its meaning: indeed Zayd did not stand, the people are affirmed as standing. ﴿Except one who has wronged, then substitutes good after evil﴾, so God has granted him security by His promise of forgiveness and mercy, and has placed him among the count of the messengers in whose presence no one fears. Some of the grammarians of Basra said: "illā" was used in this place because "illā" enters into such speech, like the saying of the Arabs: "I do not complain except of good", so he did not make His saying "except good" about complaint, but he knew that when he says "I do not complain of anything" he mentions good about himself; as if he said: "I do not mention except good".

And some of the grammarians of Kufa said: someone says: how is one who fears because of wrongdoing made, then substitutes good after evil, and he is forgiven? I say to you: in this verse there are two aspects. One is that the messengers are protected, forgiven, secure on the Day of Resurrection; and whoever mixed a righteous deed with another evil one, he fears and hopes; this is one aspect. The other: that the exception is made from those left out in the word, because the meaning is: the messengers do not fear in My presence; fear is only for those other than them; then He excepted, saying: ﴿except one who has wronged, then substitutes good﴾, meaning: he was a polytheist, then repented from polytheism and did good, so that one is forgiven and does not fear. He said: some grammarians have said: "illā" in the language is in the position of "wa" (and), and the meaning of this verse is: the messengers do not fear in My presence, nor one who has wronged then substituted good. He said: they made its like His saying: ﴿So that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who have wronged﴾. He said: and I did not find that Arabic admits what they said, because I do not permit: "the people stood except ʿAbd Allah", while ʿAbd Allah is standing; the meaning of the exception is that the noun after "illā" exits from the sense of the nouns before "illā". And I see it permissible for someone to say: "I owe you a thousand besides another thousand"; if "illā" is placed in this position it is correct, and "illā" is in the sense of what they said. As for it bare, having excepted a little of the much, then no; but like it is what the meaning of "illā" is like the meaning of "wa", and it is not it: His saying ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾ is in meaning: what your Lord wills of addition. So do not make "illā" in the position of "wa", but in the position of "siwā" (besides); for when "siwā" is in the place of "illā", it is correct in the sense of "wa", because you say: "I have much wealth besides this", i.e. and this is with me, as if you said: "I have much wealth and this also is with me"; and it is further in "siwā" than in "illā", because you say: "with me is besides this", and you do not say: "with me is except this".

Abu Jaʿfar said: The correct statement regarding His saying ﴿except one who has wronged, then substitutes﴾ in my view is other than what these people of Arabic whose sayings we have related said; rather it is the statement said by al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Juraij, and whoever said their statement, which is that His saying: ﴿except one who has been wronged﴾ is a correct exception from His saying ﴿the messengers do not fear in My presence, except one who has wronged﴾ among them, who committed a sin; for he is fearful in His presence of His punishment. And al-Hasan, may God have mercy on him, clarified the meaning of God's saying that to Moses, which is his saying: indeed I only frightened you because of your killing of a soul.

If someone says: what is the reasoning of His saying, if His saying ﴿except one who has been wronged﴾ is a correct exception and outside the count of those messengers who do not fear in His presence, and how can one who has been promised forgiveness and mercy be fearful? It is said: His saying ﴿then substitutes good after evil﴾ is another statement after the first, and the report about the messengers who wronged among them has ended, and about those among them who did not wrong at His saying ﴿except one who has been wronged﴾; then He began the report about those among the messengers who wronged, and the rest of people other than them; and it is said: so whoever wronged, then substituted good after evil, indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful to him.

If someone says: then why is "thumma" (then) attached if it is not a conjunction to His saying ﴿wronged﴾? It is said: it is upon something left out, sufficed by the indication of His saying ﴿then substitutes good after evil﴾ from mentioning it, since a similar thing has already occurred before in the speech, namely: "so whoever of creation wronged". As for those whose statements from the people of Arabic we have mentioned, they spoke according to the way of Arabic, except that they overlooked the meaning of the word and carried it upon other than its interpretive direction. Rather, speech should be carried upon its correct interpretive direction, and for its grammatical construction a sound outlet should be sought in that direction, not by diverting the word from its meaning and its correct interpretive direction.

* *

And His saying: ﴿then substitutes good after evil﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: so whoever among God's creation commits wrongdoing and incurs sin, then substitutes good, i.e. then repents from that wrongdoing and incurring of sin, ﴿indeed I am Forgiving﴾, meaning: indeed I cover over his sin and that wrongdoing by My pardon, and by leaving off punishing him for it, ﴿Merciful﴾ to him, that I would punish him after his substituting good for its opposite.

And in accordance with what we have said regarding this, the people of interpretation said.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, he said: Abu ʿĀṣim narrated to us, he said: ʿĪsā narrated to us; and al-Ḥārith narrated to me, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Warqāʾ narrated to us, all of them, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿except one who has wronged, then substitutes good after evil﴾, then repented after his wrongdoing: ﴿indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 9–11:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Moses, indeed it is I, Allah, the Almighty, the Wise﴾ (9) ﴿And throw down your staff.﴾ So when he saw it moving as if it were a snake (jann), he turned back in retreat and did not return. ﴿O Moses, do not fear. Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾ (10) ﴿except one who has wronged; then substitutes good after evil — indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (11)

He, exalted is His remembrance, says, reporting His speech to Moses: ﴿Indeed, it is I, Allah, the Almighty﴾ in His vengeance against His enemies, ﴿the Wise﴾ in His management of His creation. The particle ha' in His saying ﴿innahu﴾ is the hā' of ʿimād (the pronoun of support, dummy pronoun), and it is a word that does not appear in the view of some of the people of Arabic grammar. And one of the grammarians of Kufa said: it is the unknown hā' (hā' al-majhūla), and its meaning is: the matter and the affair is: I am Allah.

* *

And His saying: ﴿And throw down your staff. So when he saw it moving﴾

In the speech there is an omitted element whose mention has been left out, being sufficed by what is mentioned over what has been omitted, and it is: so he threw it down, and it became a snake moving. ﴿So when he saw it moving as if it were a jann﴾ means: as if it were a great snake. And the jann is a species of snakes known.

Ibn Juraij said concerning this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, he said: Ibn Juraij said regarding ﴿And throw down your staff. So when he saw it moving as if it were a jann﴾: when it turned into a snake running. And this species of snakes is what the rajiz (poet) meant by his saying:

They raise, at night when it darkens, necks of jinn-snakes and trembling heads,
And a necks after the ar-rasim, swift (khaṭafā)

[These are three verses of mashtūr rajaz by al-Khaṭafī, who is Ḥudhayfa ibn Badr, grandfather of Jarir ibn ʿAṭiyya, the poet of Tamim, describing his camels and their march at night. Asdafa: grew dark. The jannān is a species of snakes which, when they move, raise their heads; and the hāmm is the plural of hāmma. The rujaf is the plural of rājifa, i.e. agitated, because of their trembling in motion and speed. The ʿanaq is a kind of fast pace. The rasīm is a light pace. The khayṭaf is quick; it is also narrated as khaṭafā, and with this Ḥudhayfa, grandfather of Jarir, was given the epithet al-Khaṭafī, because the word came in his poetry and in (Lisān, kh-ṭ-f). The khayṭafī means the quickness of the pace being pulled, as if it snatches its neck in its walk, i.e. drags it; and a camel khayṭaf means swift in passing, and it is said ʿanaq khayṭaf and khaṭafī; the grandfather of Jarir said: "and a neck after the rasīm, khayṭafā". It was also said that it derives from al-khaṭf, which is snatching, and a camel khayṭaf is one whose pace is like that, i.e. swift in passing.]]

And His saying: ﴿He turned back in retreat﴾ means, He, exalted is His remembrance: Moses turned away fleeeing in fear of it. ﴿And did not return﴾ means: he did not come back. From the saying of the people: ʿaqaba fulān, when he returned upon his heels to where he started.

And in accordance with what we have said regarding the interpretation of this, the people of interpretation said.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, he said: Abu ʿĀṣim narrated to us, he said: ʿĪsā narrated to us; and al-Ḥārith narrated to me, he said: al-Ḥasan narrated to us, he said: Warqāʾ narrated to us, all of them, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of God: ﴿And did not return﴾, he said: he did not return.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, similarly.

He said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Abu Sufyan narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatada, he said: he did not look back.

Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿And did not return﴾, he said: he did not return. ﴿O Moses﴾, he said: when he threw down the staff it became a snake, so he was frightened by it and became distressed, so God said: ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾. He said: so he did not heed that. He said: So God said to him: ﴿Come forward and do not fear; indeed, you are among the secure﴾. He said: so he did not stop at any of this until He said: ﴿We will return it to its original form﴾. He said: so he looked, and behold, it was a staff as it had been, so he returned and took it, and then he became strong after that until he was sending it against Pharaoh and taking it.

* *

And His saying: ﴿O Moses, do not fear. Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence, except one who has wronged﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: So his Lord called to him: O Moses, do not fear this snake; indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence. He means: indeed, My messengers and prophets whom I have singled out with prophethood do not fear in My presence, except whoever among them has wronged, acting otherwise than what He permitted him to act upon.

And in accordance with what we have said regarding this, the people of interpretation said.

And His saying: ﴿then substitutes good after evil﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: so whoever among God's creation commits wrongdoing and incurs sin, then substitutes good, i.e. then repents from that wrongdoing and incurring of sin, ﴿indeed I am Forgiving﴾, meaning: indeed I cover over his sin and that wrongdoing by My pardon, and by leaving off punishing him for it, ﴿Merciful﴾ to him, that I would punish him after his substituting good for its opposite.

And in accordance with what we have said regarding this, the people of interpretation said.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, he said: Abu ʿĀṣim narrated to us, he said: ʿĪsā narrated to us; and al-Ḥārith narrated to me, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Warqāʾ narrated to us, all of them, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿except one who has wronged, then substitutes good after evil﴾, then repented after his wrongdoing: ﴿indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

The Interpretation of His Words, the Exalted: ﴿And put your hand into your bosom; it will come out white, without disease, among nine signs to Pharaoh and his people. Indeed, they have been a defiantly disobedient people.﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says, relating what He said to His prophet Musa: ﴿And put your hand into your bosom﴾. It is mentioned that He, may His remembrance be exalted, commanded him to put his palm into his bosom. He commanded him to insert it into his bosom because what he was wearing at that time was a woolen robe (midra'a). Some of them said: it had no sleeves. Others said: its sleeve reached to part of his hand.

Mention of those who said that:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿And put your hand into your bosom﴾: he said, "Only the palm, into your bosom." He said: "It was a robe reaching to part of his hand; and if it had had a sleeve, He would have commanded him to put his hand into its sleeve."

He said: Hajjaj related to me, from Yunus ibn Abi Ishaq, from his father, from Amr ibn Maymun, who said: Ibn Mas'ud said: "Musa came to Pharaoh when he came to him wearing a dhurmanaqa," meaning a woolen cloak (jubba).

* *

As for His words, ﴿it will come out white﴾:

He says: the hand will come out white, not with the colour of Musa's skin, ﴿without disease﴾, meaning: without leprosy (baras). ﴿Among nine signs﴾: He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: put your hand into your bosom; it will come out white, without disease, so it is a sign among nine signs with which you are being sent to Pharaoh. The mention of "sent" has been omitted because the words ﴿to Pharaoh and his people﴾ indicate that this is its meaning, as the poet said:

She saw me with her two ropes and turned away out of fear,
And in the rope was a fearful heart, a timid one...

The meaning of the verse is: she saw me approaching with her two ropes; so the word "approaching" was omitted, since the listeners understood its meaning from her saying "she saw me with her two ropes." Parallels of this in the speech of the Arabs are numerous.

As for the nine signs, they are those which we have explained earlier.

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words, ﴿among nine signs to Pharaoh and his people﴾: "They are those which God mentioned in the Qur'an: the staff, the hand, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the flood, the blood, the stone, and the obliteration which befell the family of Pharaoh in their wealth."

* *

As for His words, ﴿Indeed, they have been a defiantly disobedient people﴾:

He says: indeed Pharaoh and his people, of the Copts, have been a defiantly disobedient people, meaning disbelievers in God; and we have explained the meaning of fisq (defiant disobedience) earlier.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 13–14:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿So when Our signs came to them, visible, they said, "This is clear magic." (13) And they denied them, while their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance. So see how was the end of the corrupters.﴾ (14)

Says God, may His remembrance be exalted: "When Our signs came to Pharaoh," meaning: Our proofs and arguments, confirming the truth of what Moses called them to and his veracity, and they are the nine signs we mentioned earlier.

* *

And His saying ﴿visible﴾:

It means: whoever looks at them and sees them makes clear through them the truth of what they indicate.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said the same as what we have said.

Those who said that:

⁕ Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: ﴿So when Our signs came to them, visible﴾ He said: clear. ﴿They said, "This is clear magic,"﴾ meaning: Pharaoh and his people said: "What Moses has brought us is clear magic," meaning: it makes it clear to those who look at it that it is magic.

* *

And His saying: ﴿And they denied them﴾

It means: they denied the nine signs that they were from God.

As:

⁕ Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: ﴿And they denied them﴾ He said: al-juhud is denying them.

* *

And His saying: ﴿while their souls were convinced of them﴾

It means: their hearts were certain of them, and they knew with certainty that they were from God, so they were obstinate after their clarification of the truth and their recognition of it.

As:

⁕ Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAtaʾ al-Khurasani, from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿while their souls were convinced of them﴾ He said: their certainty in their hearts.

⁕ Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding God's saying: ﴿while their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance﴾ He said: They were certain that the signs were truth from God, so why did they deny them? He said: "Out of injustice and arrogance."

* *

And His saying: ﴿out of injustice and arrogance﴾

By injustice is meant transgression (i'tida'), and by arrogance (ʿuluww) is meant pride (kibr), as if it were said: transgression and haughtiness.

The people of interpretation said the same as what we have said.

Those who said that:

⁕ Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding His saying: ﴿out of injustice and arrogance﴾ He said: exalting oneself and being arrogant. The meaning of that: they denied the nine signs out of injustice and arrogance, while their souls were certain that they were from God, so they opposed the truth after its clarity to them. This is from the delayed (al-mu'akhkhar) whose meaning is the advanced (al-taqdim).

* *

And His saying: ﴿So see how was the end of the corrupters﴾

.

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): "So see, O Muhammad, with the eye of your heart, how was the end of the denial of those who denied Our signs when they came to them visible, and what befell them from their corruption in the earth and their disobedience to their Lord in it. What they did brought its consequence upon them: it removed them from gardens, springs, crops and a noble station, to destruction in this world by drowning, and in the next to an everlasting punishment that will not be lightened for them, and in which they will be despairing." He says: And thus, O Muhammad, is My way with those among your people who denied what you brought them of the signs, concerning the truth to which you call them.

* *

And His saying: ﴿while their souls were convinced of them﴾

It means: their hearts were certain of them, and they knew with certainty that they were from God, so they were obstinate after their clarification of the truth and their recognition of it.

As:

⁕ Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAtaʾ al-Khurasani, from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿while their souls were convinced of them﴾ He said: their certainty in their hearts.

⁕ Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding God's saying: ﴿while their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance﴾ He said: They were certain that the signs were truth from God, so why did they deny them? He said: "Out of injustice and arrogance."

* *

And His saying: ﴿out of injustice and arrogance﴾

By injustice is meant transgression (i'tida'), and by arrogance (ʿuluww) is meant pride (kibr), as if it were said: transgression and haughtiness.

The people of interpretation said the same as what we have said.

Those who said that:

⁕ Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding His saying: ﴿out of injustice and arrogance﴾ He said: exalting oneself and being arrogant. The meaning of that: they denied the nine signs out of injustice and arrogance, while their souls were certain that they were from God, so they opposed the truth after its clarity to them. This is from the delayed (al-mu'akhkhar) whose meaning is the advanced (al-taqdim).

* *

And His saying: ﴿So see how was the end of the corrupters﴾

.

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): "So see, O Muhammad, with the eye of your heart, how was the end of the denial of those who denied Our signs when they came to them visible, and what befell them from their corruption in the earth and their disobedience to their Lord in it. What they did brought its consequence upon them: it removed them from gardens, springs, crops and a noble station, to destruction in this world by drowning, and in the next to an everlasting punishment that will not be lightened for them, and in which they will be despairing." He says: And thus, O Muhammad, is My way with those among your people who denied what you brought them of the signs, concerning the truth to which you call them.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 15–16:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly gave knowledge to David and Solomon. And they both said, "Praise be to Allah, who has favoured us over many of His believing servants."﴾ (15)

His words, exalted is His remembrance: ﴿And We certainly gave knowledge to David and Solomon﴾, and that knowledge was the knowledge of the speech of birds and beasts, and other things that Allah singled them out with knowing. ﴿And they both said, "Praise be to Allah, who has favoured us over many of His believing servants."﴾ He, may His praise be glorified, says: David and Solomon said, "Praise be to Allah who has favoured us, by means of the knowledge with which He singled us out and which He gave us, over the rest of His creation of the children of Adam in our time, over many of His servants who believe in Him in our era."

* *

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿And Solomon inherited David. And he said, "O people, we have been taught the speech of birds, and we have been given of all things. Indeed, this is evidently the bounty."﴾ (16)

His words, exalted is His remembrance: ﴿And Solomon inherited﴾ his father ﴿David﴾ the knowledge that Allah had given him during his lifetime, and the kingship that He had singled him out with over all his people, so He made it his after his father David, to the exclusion of the rest of his father's sons. ﴿And he said, "O people, we have been taught the speech of birds"﴾. He says: Solomon said to his people, "O people, we have been taught the speech of birds," meaning, we have been given understanding of their speech; and he regarded that as being from the birds, like the speech of a man of the children of Adam, since he understood it from them.

⁕ Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Abu Ma'shar, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b: ﴿And he said, "O people, we have been taught the speech of birds"﴾. He said: We have been told that Solomon's army was a hundred farsakh: twenty-five of them were for humankind, twenty-five for the jinn, twenty-five for the wild beasts, and twenty-five for the birds. He had a thousand chambers of glass upon wood, in which were three hundred female companions and seven hundred concubines. He commanded the stormy wind and it lifted him up, and commanded the gentle wind and it carried him along. Allah revealed to him, while he was travelling between heaven and earth: "Indeed, I have willed that no creature speak anything except that the wind comes and informs him."

* *

His words: ﴿And We have been given of all things﴾.

He says: We were given and granted from every thing of good. ﴿Indeed, this is evidently the bounty﴾. He says: Indeed, this which we have been given of good things is clearly the bounty over all the people of our era, he says: that which becomes clear to whoever reflects upon and contemplates it, that it is a bounty We gave to us over other people.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 15–16:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly gave knowledge to David and Solomon. And they both said, "Praise be to Allah, who has favoured us over many of His believing servants."﴾ (15)

His words, exalted is His remembrance: ﴿And We certainly gave knowledge to David and Solomon﴾, and that knowledge was the knowledge of the speech of birds and beasts, and other things that Allah singled them out with knowing. ﴿And they both said, "Praise be to Allah, who has favoured us over many of His believing servants."﴾ He, may His praise be glorified, says: David and Solomon said, "Praise be to Allah who has favoured us, by means of the knowledge with which He singled us out and which He gave us, over the rest of His creation of the children of Adam in our time, over many of His servants who believe in Him in our era."

* *

He said: We have been told that Solomon's army was a hundred farsakh: twenty-five of them were for humankind, twenty-five for the jinn, twenty-five for the wild beasts, and twenty-five for the birds. He had a thousand chambers of glass upon wood, in which were three hundred female companions and seven hundred concubines. He commanded the stormy wind and it lifted him up, and commanded the gentle wind and it carried him along. Allah revealed to him, while he was travelling between heaven and earth: "Indeed, I have willed that no creature speak anything except that the wind comes and informs him."

* *

His words: ﴿And We have been given of all things﴾.

He says: We were given and granted from every thing of good. ﴿Indeed, this is evidently the bounty﴾. He says: Indeed, this which we have been given of good things is clearly the bounty over all the people of our era, he says: that which becomes clear to whoever reflects upon and contemplates it, that it is a bounty We gave to us over other people.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 17:

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And there were gathered before Solomon his hosts of the jinn and of mankind and of the birds, and they were marshalled in ranks﴾.

He, exalted is His mention, says: And there were gathered for Solomon his hosts of the jinn, mankind and birds on a march for them, and they were marshalled in ranks.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning the meaning of His words ﴿they were marshalled in ranks﴾. Some of them said: the meaning of that is: their first is held back until their last gathers together.

Those who said that:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: a man was appointed over each category to turn back its first from its last, so that they would not get ahead of one another on the march, as kings do.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Abu Sufyan narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿And there were gathered for Solomon his hosts of the jinn, mankind and birds, and they were marshalled in ranks﴾, he said: their first is turned back upon their last.

Others said: the meaning of that is: they are driven on.

Those who said that:

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿And there were gathered for Solomon his hosts of the jinn, mankind and birds, and they were marshalled in ranks﴾, he said: "yuzda'un" means: they are driven on.

Others said: rather, its meaning is: they advance.

Those who said that:

al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Sufyan narrated to us, from Ma'mar, who said: al-Hasan said: ﴿yuza'un﴾ means they advance.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: the most correct of these opinions is the view of the one who said: its meaning is that their first is turned back upon their last. That is because al-wazi' (the restrainer) in the speech of the Arabs is the one who holds back. It is said from it: "Wazza'a fulanun fulanan 'an al-zulm" (so-and-so restrained so-and-so from wrongdoing) when he withheld him from it, as the poet said:

"Did not restraint (al-hawa) hold back, when it was not complied with... Yes, and you forgot the pursuit of the young woman."[[al-wazʻ: restraining the self from its desires. Wazaʻahu wa-bihi yazaʻu (with both fatha and kasra on the zay) wazʻan: he restrained him. Yu'at: complies. In Lisan al-'Arab: "wa'atahu 'ala al-amr": he obeyed him. Al-mu'ata: good compliance; "a'taytuhu 'ala dhalika al-amr mu'atat": when you agree with him and obey him. The common people say "wataytuhu" and do not say "wa'atayt" except in a dialect of the people of Yemen; similarly "asaytu," "akaltu," "amarti," and they made them with a waw to lighten the hamza.]]

And another said:

"When I rebuked white hair for youth, and said: 'Ah, let me sober up,' while white hair is a restrainer..."[[The verse is by al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani from a poem offering an apology to al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir (Mukhtar al-shi'r al-jahili, explained by Mustafa al-Saqqa, Halabi edition, pp. 156 ff.). "Sahâ" means he came to his senses; al-wazi' is the restrainer who turns one back from frivolity and play; al-sabwa is the youthful inclination, and the tendency to imitate the conduct of children in frivolity and play.]]

It is only said of those who push people back from the rulers and commanders: "wazaʻa" (guards/enforcers), because they restrain people from them.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 27, verse 18:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said, "O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his soldiers crush you, while they do not perceive."﴾

He, may He be exalted and remembered, means by His saying: ﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾, until Solomon and his soldiers came upon the valley of the ants. ﴿An ant said, "O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his soldiers crush you"﴾, meaning: lest Solomon and his soldiers break you and kill you. ﴿While they do not perceive﴾, meaning: while they do not know that they are crushing you.

⁕ Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, who said: Abd al-Rahman and Yahya narrated to us, the two of them saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from a man called al-Hakam, from Awf, regarding His saying: ﴿An ant said, "O ants"﴾, he said: The ants of Solomon son of David were like flies.

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿So he smiled, laughing at her words, and said, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and to do righteousness that pleases You, and admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants."﴾

He, may He be exalted and remembered, says: So Solomon smiled, laughing at the words of the ant that spoke what it spoke, and he said: ﴿My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me﴾. By His saying ﴿enable me (awzi'ni)﴾ he means: inspire me (alhamni).

The interpreters of the Qur'an have said the same as what we have said on this.

Those who said that:

⁕ Yunus narrated to me, who said: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding the words of God: ﴿My Lord, enable me (awzi'ni) to be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me﴾, he said: In the speech of the Arabs, one says: "Awza'a Fulan bi-Fulan," meaning: he urged him against him (harrada 'alayhi). And Ibn Zayd said: ﴿Awzi'ni﴾ means inspire me (alhamni) and urge me (harridni) to be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents.

* *

And His saying: ﴿and to do righteousness that pleases You﴾

He says: And enable me to work in obedience to You and what You are pleased with. ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾, he says: And admit me by Your mercy with Your righteous servants, whom You have chosen for Your message and selected for Your revelation; he means: admit me into the Garden in their dwelling places.

The interpreters of the Qur'an have said the same as what we have said on this.

Those who said that:

⁕ Yunus narrated to me, who said: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾, he said: With Your righteous servants, the prophets and the believers.

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And he inspected the birds and said, "Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?"﴾ [27:20]

He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And he [Solomon] inspected the birds and said, "Why do I not see the hoopoe?"﴾ As for the reason he inspected the birds and asked about the hoopoe in particular from among the birds, the reports are as follows:

* Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard Imran from Abu Mijlaz, who said: Ibn Abbas sat with Abdullah ibn Salam, and asked him about the hoopoe: why did Solomon inspect it from among the birds? Abdullah ibn Salam said: Solomon alighted at a place during a journey of his, and he did not know how far the water was. He said: "Who knows how far the water is?" They said: "The hoopoe." That is when he inspected it.

* Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Imran ibn Hudayr narrated to us, from Abu Mijlaz, from Ibn Abbas and Abdullah ibn Salam, with similar wording.

* Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to me, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from al-Minhal, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Solomon ibn Dawud would have six hundred thrones set out for him. Then the nobles of mankind would come and sit closest to him, then the nobles of the jinn would come and sit next to mankind. He said: Then he would call the birds, and they would shade them. Then he would call the wind, and it would carry them. He said: In a single morning it would travel the distance of a month. He said: While he was on his journey, he needed water while he was in a wilderness of the earth. He said: So he called the hoopoe, and it came and pecked the ground, and it struck the place of the water. He said: Then the devils would come and skin it (the ground) as a hide is skinned, and then they would extract the water. Nafi' ibn al-Azraq said to him: "Wait, O little stutterer! Have you seen your saying, that the hoopoe comes and pecks the ground and strikes water? How can it see this, yet it does not see the snare when it comes until it falls into its neck?" He said: Ibn Abbas said to him: "Woe to you! When the decree comes, it prevents sight."

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from some people of knowledge, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: Whenever Solomon ibn Dawud left his house for his assembly, the birds would gather around him, and the jinn and humans would stand for him until he sat upon his throne. Then one morning during some period of his life, he went to the assembly where he used to sit, and he inspected the birds. It is claimed that a bird from every species of bird would come to him in turn. He looked and saw that all species of birds had come to him except the hoopoe. So he said: "Why do I not see the hoopoe?"

* Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: The first time Solomon missed the hoopoe, he alighted in a valley and asked mankind about its water. They said: "We do not know of any water for it. If any of your soldiers knows of water for it, (it would be) the jinn." He called the jinn and asked them. They said: "We do not know of any water for it. If any of your soldiers knows of water for it, (it would be) the birds." He called the birds and asked them. They said: "We do not know of any water for it. If any of your soldiers knows of it, (it would be) the hoopoe." But he did not find it. He said: That was the first time the hoopoe was missed.

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And he inspected the birds and said, "Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?"﴾ He said: He inspected the hoopoe because it used to guide him to water when he rode. One day Solomon rode and said: "Where is the hoopoe, so that it may guide us to the water?" He did not find it, and so he inspected it for this reason. Ibn Abbas said: The hoopoe used to benefit from caution as long as its term had not come. When its term came, caution did not benefit it, and the decree came between it and sight.

Abdullah ibn Salam, those who held his view, and Wahb ibn Munabbih differed. Abdullah said: The reason for his inspecting the hoopoe and asking about it was to learn from it how far the water was in the valley where he had alighted during his journey. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: His inspecting it and asking about it was because it had failed to fulfil the turn (duty) it was assigned. Allah knows best which of these was the case, since no revelation has come to us about which of them it was, nor is there any authentic report from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The correct view on this matter is to say: Allah informed us that Solomon inspected the birds, either because of the turn (duty) that was assigned to the hoopoe and which it neglected, or because of a need he had for it regarding the distance of the water.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿And he said, "Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?"﴾

By His saying ﴿Why do I not see the hoopoe?﴾ he means: "My sight has missed it, so I do not see it, though it should be present; or is it absent, among the other kinds of creatures that are absent and not present?"

Those who engage in ta'wil (interpretation) have said the like of what we have said on this.

Mention of those who said this:

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from some people of knowledge, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, regarding ﴿Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?﴾ "My sight missed it among the birds, or is it absent and not present?"

* *

As for His saying: ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾

He says: When Solomon was informed about the hoopoe that it was not present, and that it was absent and not witnessing, he swore: ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment.﴾ It is reported that his punishment of the birds, when he punished them, was to pluck out their feathers.

Those who engage in ta'wil have said the like of what we have said on this.

Mention of those who said this:

* Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: al-Hammani narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from al-Minhal, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾: "He plucked out its feathers."

* Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Atiyyah narrated to us, from Sharik, from Ata', from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾: "His punishment is plucking it and exposing it to the sun."

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾: "He plucked out its feathers and exposed it to the sun."

* Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾: "He plucked out all of its feathers."

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: "He plucked out all the feathers of the hoopoe, so that it would not sleep even a little."

* He said: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Sufyan narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, who said: "He plucked out its feathers."

* It was narrated to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say, regarding His saying: ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾: "He plucked out its feathers."

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to me, from Yazid ibn Ruman, that he reported that his punishment with which he punished the birds was plucking its wing.

* Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: It was said to some people of knowledge: "This is slaughter, so what is the severe punishment?" He said: "Plucking its feathers, leaving it as a piece of flesh that writhes."

* Sa'id ibn al-Rabi' al-Razi narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Amr ibn Bashshar, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾: "He plucked it."

* Sa'id ibn al-Rabi' narrated to me, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Husayn ibn Abi Shaddad, who said: "He plucked it and exposed it to the sun." ﴿Or I will surely slaughter him﴾ means: "Or I will surely kill him."

As well as:

* It was narrated to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say, regarding His saying: ﴿Or I will surely slaughter him﴾: "He means: or I will surely kill him."

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abbad ibn al-Awwam narrated to us, from Husayn, from Abdullah ibn Shaddad: ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or I will surely slaughter him﴾ ... the verse. He said: The birds met him and informed him, and he said: "Did he not make an exception?"

* *

As for His saying: ﴿Or he must bring me a clear authority﴾

He means: "Or he must bring me a proof that makes clear to the hearer its soundness and reality."

Those who engage in ta'wil have said the like of what we have said on this.

Mention of those who said this:

* Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Azdi narrated to us, saying: al-Mu'afa ibn Imran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ammar al-Duhni, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Every 'sultan' (authority) in the Qur'an is a proof."

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Or he must bring me a clear authority﴾: "He means: with a clear evidence by which I may excuse him. It is like His saying: ﴿Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without any authority﴾, meaning: without any evidence."

* Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from a man, from Ikrimah, who said: "Every 'sultan' in the Qur'an is a proof."

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abdullah ibn Yazid narrated to us, from Qabath [[Qabath, pronounced like Sahab, son of Rizin al-Lakhmi (also said: al-Tujibi). Qabath is an Arabic name.]] ibn Rizin, that he heard Ikrimah say: I heard Ibn Abbas say: "Every 'sultan' in the Qur'an is a proof. The hoopoe had a 'sultan'."

* al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Sufyan narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿Or he must bring me a clear authority﴾: "A clear excuse."

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from some people of knowledge, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, regarding ﴿Or he must bring me a clear authority﴾: "That is, a proof that excused him for his absence."

* It was narrated to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say, regarding His saying: ﴿Or he must bring me a clear authority﴾: "He means: with a clear evidence, and this is the saying of Allah: ﴿Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without any authority﴾, meaning: without any evidence."

* Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿Or he must bring me a clear authority﴾: "With an excuse he may make for it."

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And he inspected the birds and said, "Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?"﴾ [27:20]

He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And he [Solomon] inspected the birds and said, "Why do I not see the hoopoe?"﴾ As for the reason he inspected the birds and asked about the hoopoe in particular from among the birds, the reports are as follows:

* Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard Imran from Abu Mijlaz, who said: Ibn Abbas sat with Abdullah ibn Salam, and asked him about the hoopoe: why did Solomon inspect it from among the birds? Abdullah ibn Salam said: Solomon alighted at a place during a journey of his, and he did not know how far the water was. He said: "Who knows how far the water is?" They said: "The hoopoe." That is when he inspected it.

* Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Imran ibn Hudayr narrated to us, from Abu Mijlaz, from Ibn Abbas and Abdullah ibn Salam, with similar wording.
